title: 10. Security & Auth: Authentication & Authorization
summary: Key Concept: Hashing is a ONE-WAY function. You can convert password → hash, but you CANNOT convert hash → password.
objectives: Everything You Need to Know About Securing Your Application

sections.title: 1. What is Authentication vs Authorization?
sections.body:
### The Restaurant Analogy 🍽️

```
Authentication = "PROVE WHO YOU ARE"
    → Showing your ID at the door
    → "Yes, you are John Smith"

Authorization = "WHAT ARE YOU ALLOWED TO DO?"
    → VIP gets the private room, regular guest gets the main hall
    → "John, you have access to the free tier, not the premium features"
```

### Real-World Examples

| Platform      | Authentication                 | Authorization                                             |
| ------------- | ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| **ChatGPT**   | Email/password or Google login | Free users: GPT-3.5, Plus users: GPT-4                    |
| **Amazon**    | Email/password + 2FA           | Buyer can buy, Seller can list, Admin can ban             |
| **Instagram** | Phone/email + password         | Public profiles: anyone views, Private: only followers    |
| **GitHub**    | Password + SSH keys            | Owner: full access, Collaborator: push, Public: read-only |

### The Authentication Flow (Every App Does This)

```
┌──────────┐     1. Send credentials      ┌──────────┐
│          │ ──────────────────────────►   │          │
│  Client  │     (email + password)        │  Server  │
│ (Browser │                               │          │
│  or App) │     2. Verify credentials     │          │
│          │ ◄──────────────────────────   │          │
│          │     (Send back token/cookie)   │          │
│          │                               │          │
│          │     3. Future requests         │          │
│          │ ──────────────────────────►   │          │
│          │     (Include token/cookie)     │          │
│          │                               │          │
│          │     4. Verify token,           │          │
│          │        return data             │          │
│          │ ◄──────────────────────────   │          │
└──────────┘                               └──────────┘
```

diagrams.title: Session cookies vs JWT access tokens
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant A as API
  participant S as Session store
  B->>A: POST /login (password)
  alt session-based
    A->>S: save session id → user
    A-->>B: Set-Cookie: sid (HttpOnly)
    B->>A: request + cookie
    A->>S: look up sid
  else JWT
    A-->>B: signed access token (15 min) + refresh token
    B->>A: Authorization: Bearer token
    A->>A: verify signature locally — no lookup
  end
diagrams.explain: **Sessions** keep state on the server: easy to revoke, but every request needs a session-store lookup. **JWTs** carry signed claims, so any server can verify them without a database call — good for scaling and microservices — but they cannot be revoked before expiry, which is why access tokens are short-lived and paired with refresh tokens. Authorization (what you may do) is checked after either.

sections.title: 2. How Passwords Work
sections.body:
### ❌ NEVER Store Plain Text Passwords

```python
# ❌ TERRIBLE - Never do this
users_db = {
    "john": "mypassword123"  # If DB is hacked, all passwords are exposed!
}
```

### ✅ How It Actually Works: Hashing

```
Password: "mypassword123"
    │
    ▼ (Hash Function - ONE WAY, cannot reverse)
    │
Hash: "$2b$12$LJ3m4ys3Gz5kGeRgFOsCzO8kJSMGeFqLTO2kfy3mFTHo7SeDzSjay"
```

**Key Concept:** Hashing is a ONE-WAY function. You can convert password → hash, but you CANNOT convert hash → password.

### How Login Verification Works

```python
# When user REGISTERS:
password = "mypassword123"
hashed = bcrypt.hash(password)
# Store hashed in database: "$2b$12$LJ3m4ys..."

# When user LOGS IN:
password_attempt = "mypassword123"
stored_hash = "$2b$12$LJ3m4ys..."
is_valid = bcrypt.verify(password_attempt, stored_hash)  # True!

# Wrong password:
wrong_attempt = "wrongpassword"
is_valid = bcrypt.verify(wrong_attempt, stored_hash)  # False!
```

### What is "Salt"?

```
Without salt:
  "password123" → always produces "abc...xyz"
  If two users have same password, they have same hash! (Bad!)

With salt (random string added):
  "password123" + "random_salt_1" → "def...uvw"
  "password123" + "random_salt_2" → "ghi...rst"
  Same password, different hashes! (Good!)
```

**bcrypt automatically handles salting for you.**

### Python Implementation

```python
from passlib.context import CryptContext

# Create password hashing context
pwd_context = CryptContext(schemes=["bcrypt"], deprecated="auto")

# Hash a password (for registration)
def hash_password(password: str) -> str:
    return pwd_context.hash(password)

# Verify a password (for login)
def verify_password(plain_password: str, hashed_password: str) -> bool:
    return pwd_context.verify(plain_password, hashed_password)

# Example
hashed = hash_password("mypassword123")
print(hashed)  # $2b$12$...something long...

print(verify_password("mypassword123", hashed))  # True
print(verify_password("wrongpassword", hashed))   # False
```

sections.title: 3. Session-Based Authentication
sections.body:
### How It Works (Traditional Web Apps)

```
┌──────────┐                              ┌──────────┐
│  Browser  │  1. POST /login              │  Server   │
│           │  {email, password}           │           │
│           │ ─────────────────────────►   │  Verifies │
│           │                              │  password │
│           │  2. Set-Cookie: session_id=  │           │
│           │     abc123                   │  Stores   │
│           │ ◄─────────────────────────   │  session  │
│           │                              │  in Redis │
│           │  3. GET /profile             │           │
│           │  Cookie: session_id=abc123   │           │
│           │ ─────────────────────────►   │  Looks up │
│           │                              │  session  │
│           │  4. {user: "John", ...}      │  in Redis │
│           │ ◄─────────────────────────   │           │
└──────────┘                              └──────────┘
```

### Session Storage

```
Server-side session store (Redis):
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Session ID: "abc123"                          │
│  Data: {                                       │
│    "user_id": 42,                              │
│    "email": "john@example.com",                │
│    "role": "admin",                            │
│    "created_at": "2026-01-15T10:00:00",        │
│    "expires_at": "2026-01-15T22:00:00"         │
│  }                                             │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Pros and Cons

| ✅ Pros                                         | ❌ Cons                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Server controls sessions (can revoke instantly) | Requires server-side storage (memory/Redis) |
| Session data not exposed to client              | Hard to scale across multiple servers       |
| Built-in browser cookie support                 | Not ideal for mobile apps or APIs           |
| Simple to implement                             | Stateful (server must remember sessions)    |

### Flask Session Example

```python
from flask import Flask, session, request, jsonify
from datetime import timedelta

app = Flask(__name__)
app.secret_key = "your-secret-key-here"
app.permanent_session_lifetime = timedelta(hours=12)

@app.route("/login", methods=["POST"])
def login():
    data = request.json
    # Verify credentials (simplified)
    user = verify_user(data["email"], data["password"])
    if user:
        session.permanent = True
        session["user_id"] = user.id
        session["role"] = user.role
        return jsonify({"message": "Logged in!"})
    return jsonify({"error": "Invalid credentials"}), 401

@app.route("/profile")
def profile():
    if "user_id" not in session:
        return jsonify({"error": "Not authenticated"}), 401
    return jsonify({"user_id": session["user_id"]})

@app.route("/logout", methods=["POST"])
def logout():
    session.clear()
    return jsonify({"message": "Logged out!"})
```

sections.title: 4. Token-Based Authentication (JWT)
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Dependency: Get Current User
- Only admins can access

**Defines:** `User`, `TokenData`, `create_access_token()`, `verify_token()`, `get_current_user()`, `require_admin()`, `login()`, `profile()`, `admin_dashboard()`

### This is what modern APIs use (FastAPI, mobile apps, SPAs)

### What is JWT?

**JWT = JSON Web Token** — A self-contained token that holds user info.

```
eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo0MiwiZW1haWwiOiJqb2huQGV4YW1wbGUuY29tIiwicm9sZSI6ImFkbWluIiwiZXhwIjoxNzA5ODk5MjAwfQ.abc123signature
```

### JWT Structure (Three Parts, Separated by Dots)

```
HEADER.PAYLOAD.SIGNATURE

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ HEADER (Algorithm & Token Type)              │
│ {                                            │
│   "alg": "HS256",                           │
│   "typ": "JWT"                              │
│ }                                            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PAYLOAD (User Data / Claims)                 │
│ {                                            │
│   "user_id": 42,                            │
│   "email": "john@example.com",              │
│   "role": "admin",                          │
│   "exp": 1709899200  ← Expiration time      │
│ }                                            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ SIGNATURE (Verification)                     │
│ HMACSHA256(                                  │
│   base64(header) + "." + base64(payload),   │
│   SECRET_KEY                                │
│ )                                            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### How JWT Authentication Works

```
┌──────────┐                              ┌──────────┐
│  Client   │  1. POST /login              │  Server   │
│           │  {email, password}           │           │
│           │ ─────────────────────────►   │  Creates  │
│           │                              │  JWT      │
│           │  2. {"token": "eyJ..."}      │  token    │
│           │ ◄─────────────────────────   │           │
│           │                              │           │
│  Stores   │  3. GET /profile             │           │
│  token    │  Authorization: Bearer eyJ.. │           │
│  locally  │ ─────────────────────────►   │  Decodes  │
│           │                              │  & verify │
│           │  4. {user: "John", ...}      │  JWT      │
│           │ ◄─────────────────────────   │  (NO DB   │
│           │                              │   lookup!)│
└──────────┘                              └──────────┘
```

### Why JWT is Great for Scalability

```
Session-Based (Stateful):
┌─────────┐     ┌─────────┐     ┌─────────┐
│ Server 1 │     │ Server 2 │     │ Server 3 │
│ Sessions:│     │ Sessions:│     │ Sessions:│
│ user_42 ✓│     │ ??? ✗   │     │ ??? ✗   │
└─────────┘     └─────────┘     └─────────┘
Problem: User logged in on Server 1, but load balancer
sends next request to Server 2 — session not found!

JWT-Based (Stateless):
┌─────────┐     ┌─────────┐     ┌─────────┐
│ Server 1 │     │ Server 2 │     │ Server 3 │
│ Has      │     │ Has      │     │ Has      │
│ SECRET   │     │ SECRET   │     │ SECRET   │
│ KEY ✓    │     │ KEY ✓    │     │ KEY ✓    │
└─────────┘     └─────────┘     └─────────┘
Any server can verify the JWT — no shared session store needed!
```

### Access Token + Refresh Token Pattern

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                        │
│  Access Token (Short-lived: 15-30 minutes)             │
│  ├── Used for every API request                        │
│  ├── Contains user_id, role, etc.                      │
│  └── If stolen, attacker has limited time              │
│                                                        │
│  Refresh Token (Long-lived: 7-30 days)                 │
│  ├── Stored in HTTP-only cookie or secure storage      │
│  ├── Used ONLY to get new access tokens                │
│  └── Stored in database (can be revoked)               │
│                                                        │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Flow:
1. Login → Get access_token (15min) + refresh_token (7 days)
2. Make API calls with access_token
3. Access token expires after 15 min
4. Send refresh_token to /refresh endpoint
5. Get new access_token
6. If refresh_token is expired → User must login again
```

### FastAPI JWT Implementation

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer, OAuth2PasswordRequestForm
from jose import JWTError, jwt
from passlib.context import CryptContext
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from pydantic import BaseModel

# Configuration
SECRET_KEY = "your-secret-key-change-in-production"
ALGORITHM = "HS256"
ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES = 30

app = FastAPI()
pwd_context = CryptContext(schemes=["bcrypt"], deprecated="auto")
oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="login")

# ──── Models ────
class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    email: str
    role: str
    hashed_password: str

class TokenData(BaseModel):
    user_id: int
    email: str
    role: str

# ──── Fake Database ────
fake_users_db = {
    "john@example.com": User(
        id=1,
        email="john@example.com",
        role="admin",
        hashed_password=pwd_context.hash("password123")
    )
}

# ──── Helper Functions ────
def create_access_token(data: dict, expires_delta: timedelta = None):
    to_encode = data.copy()
    expire = datetime.utcnow() + (expires_delta or timedelta(minutes=15))
    to_encode.update({"exp": expire})
    return jwt.encode(to_encode, SECRET_KEY, algorithm=ALGORITHM)

def verify_token(token: str) -> TokenData:
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(token, SECRET_KEY, algorithms=[ALGORITHM])
        return TokenData(
            user_id=payload["user_id"],
            email=payload["email"],
            role=payload["role"]
        )
    except JWTError:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
            detail="Invalid token"
        )

# ──── Dependency: Get Current User ────
async def get_current_user(token: str = Depends(oauth2_scheme)) -> TokenData:
    return verify_token(token)

# Only admins can access
async def require_admin(user: TokenData = Depends(get_current_user)):
    if user.role != "admin":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Admin access required")
    return user

# ──── Routes ────
@app.post("/login")
async def login(form_data: OAuth2PasswordRequestForm = Depends()):
    user = fake_users_db.get(form_data.username)
    if not user or not pwd_context.verify(form_data.password, user.hashed_password):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Invalid credentials")

    token = create_access_token({
        "user_id": user.id,
        "email": user.email,
        "role": user.role
    })
    return {"access_token": token, "token_type": "bearer"}

@app.get("/profile")
async def profile(user: TokenData = Depends(get_current_user)):
    return {"user_id": user.user_id, "email": user.email, "role": user.role}

@app.get("/admin/dashboard")
async def admin_dashboard(user: TokenData = Depends(require_admin)):
    return {"message": f"Welcome admin {user.email}!"}
```

sections.title: 5. OAuth 2.0
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- User_info["name"] = "John Smith"
- Create or find user in YOUR database
- Generate YOUR JWT token

**Defines:** `login_google()`, `auth_callback()`

### "Login with Google" — How Does It Work?

```
You've seen these buttons everywhere:
┌──────────────────────────┐
│  🔵 Continue with Google  │
│  ⬛ Continue with GitHub  │
│  🔵 Continue with Facebook│
│  📧 Sign up with Email    │
└──────────────────────────┘
```

### The OAuth 2.0 Flow (Authorization Code Grant)

```
┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐
│  Your App │     │  Google   │     │  Your    │
│ (Client)  │     │ (Auth     │     │  Server  │
│           │     │  Provider)│     │  (API)   │
└─────┬─────┘     └─────┬─────┘     └────┬─────┘
      │                 │                │
      │ 1. User clicks "Login with      │
      │    Google" button               │
      ├────────────────►│                │
      │                 │                │
      │ 2. Google shows login page       │
      │◄────────────────┤                │
      │                 │                │
      │ 3. User enters Google            │
      │    email/password                │
      ├────────────────►│                │
      │                 │                │
      │ 4. Google asks: "Allow           │
      │    YourApp to access             │
      │    your profile?"                │
      │◄────────────────┤                │
      │                 │                │
      │ 5. User clicks "Allow"          │
      ├────────────────►│                │
      │                 │                │
      │ 6. Google redirects to your      │
      │    app with authorization_code   │
      │◄────────────────┤                │
      │                 │                │
      │ 7. Your server sends code +      │
      │    client_secret to Google       │
      │                 ├───────────────►│
      │                 │                │
      │ 8. Google returns access_token   │
      │                 │◄───────────────┤
      │                 │                │
      │ 9. Your server uses token to     │
      │    get user profile from Google  │
      │                 ├───────────────►│
      │                 │                │
      │ 10. Create user account or       │
      │     login existing user          │
      │◄────────────────────────────────┤
      │                 │                │
```

### OAuth 2.0 Key Concepts

```
Client ID     = Your app's public identifier (safe to expose)
Client Secret = Your app's private key (NEVER expose!)
Redirect URI  = Where Google sends the user back after login
Scope         = What permissions your app is requesting
                e.g., "email profile" = just email and name
                       "email profile drive" = also Google Drive access
Access Token  = Token to access Google APIs on behalf of user
```

### Why Use OAuth?

```
Without OAuth:
  User must create new account → New password to remember
  You must store/protect their password → Security liability
  User doesn't trust giving password to unknown app

With OAuth:
  User logs in with existing Google/GitHub → No new password
  You NEVER see their Google password → Less liability
  User trusts Google's login page → Higher sign-up rate
```

### FastAPI OAuth Example (Google Login)

```python
from authlib.integrations.starlette_client import OAuth
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from starlette.middleware.sessions import SessionMiddleware

app = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(SessionMiddleware, secret_key="secret")

oauth = OAuth()
oauth.register(
    name='google',
    client_id='YOUR_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID',
    client_secret='YOUR_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET',
    server_metadata_url='https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration',
    client_kwargs={'scope': 'openid email profile'}
)

@app.get("/login/google")
async def login_google(request: Request):
    redirect_uri = request.url_for("auth_callback")
    return await oauth.google.authorize_redirect(request, redirect_uri)

@app.get("/auth/callback")
async def auth_callback(request: Request):
    token = await oauth.google.authorize_access_token(request)
    user_info = token.get("userinfo")

    # Now you have:
    # user_info["email"] = "john@gmail.com"
    # user_info["name"] = "John Smith"
    # user_info["picture"] = "https://..."

    # Create or find user in YOUR database
    # Generate YOUR JWT token
    # Return to client

    return {"email": user_info["email"], "name": user_info["name"]}
```

sections.title: 6. API Key Authentication
sections.body:
### The Simplest Auth Method (For Server-to-Server Communication)

```
How APIs like OpenAI, Stripe, SendGrid work:

1. You sign up → Dashboard gives you an API key
2. You include the key in every request

curl https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-abc123your-api-key" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "gpt-4", "messages": [...]}'
```

### When to Use What

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   AUTHENTICATION METHODS                  │
├──────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Method           │ Best For                              │
├──────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────┤
│ JWT Tokens       │ Mobile apps, SPAs, microservices      │
│ Sessions/Cookies │ Traditional server-rendered web apps  │
│ OAuth 2.0        │ "Login with Google/GitHub" buttons    │
│ API Keys         │ Server-to-server, third-party APIs    │
│ Basic Auth       │ Simple internal tools (avoid in prod) │
└──────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────┘
```

sections.title: 7. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
sections.body:
### How Amazon Manages Millions of Users with Different Permissions

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ RBAC Model                                               │
│                                                          │
│ User → Role → Permissions                                │
│                                                          │
│ John → Admin → [create, read, update, delete, ban_users] │
│ Jane → Seller → [create_product, read, update_own]       │
│ Bob  → Buyer → [read, create_order, write_review]        │
│ Eve  → Moderator → [read, delete_review, ban_users]      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### E-commerce RBAC Example

```python
from enum import Enum
from functools import wraps
from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException

class Role(str, Enum):
    ADMIN = "admin"
    SELLER = "seller"
    BUYER = "buyer"
    MODERATOR = "moderator"

# Permission definitions
ROLE_PERMISSIONS = {
    Role.ADMIN: ["*"],  # Everything
    Role.SELLER: [
        "product:create", "product:read", "product:update_own", "product:delete_own",
        "order:read_own", "analytics:read_own"
    ],
    Role.BUYER: [
        "product:read", "order:create", "order:read_own",
        "review:create", "review:update_own", "cart:manage"
    ],
    Role.MODERATOR: [
        "product:read", "review:read", "review:delete",
        "user:read", "user:ban"
    ]
}

def has_permission(role: Role, permission: str) -> bool:
    perms = ROLE_PERMISSIONS.get(role, [])
    return "*" in perms or permission in perms

# FastAPI dependency
def require_permission(permission: str):
    async def checker(user: TokenData = Depends(get_current_user)):
        if not has_permission(user.role, permission):
            raise HTTPException(
                status_code=403,
                detail=f"Permission '{permission}' required"
            )
        return user
    return checker

# Usage in routes
@app.post("/products")
async def create_product(
    product: ProductCreate,
    user: TokenData = Depends(require_permission("product:create"))
):
    return {"message": "Product created!", "seller_id": user.user_id}

@app.delete("/reviews/{review_id}")
async def delete_review(
    review_id: int,
    user: TokenData = Depends(require_permission("review:delete"))
):
    return {"message": f"Review {review_id} deleted by moderator"}
```

sections.title: 8. How Real Apps Do It
sections.body:
### ChatGPT / Claude Authentication

```
1. User signs up with email/password OR Google OAuth
2. Server creates user record in PostgreSQL
3. Server returns JWT access_token (short-lived) + refresh_token (in HTTP-only cookie)
4. Every API call includes: Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
5. When access_token expires → client calls /refresh with refresh_token
6. Rate limiting per user tier (Free: 25 msgs/3hrs, Plus: Higher limits)
7. API keys (sk-...) for developer API access with usage-based billing
```

### Instagram Authentication

```
1. User signs up (email/phone + password, or Facebook OAuth)
2. Password hashed with bcrypt, stored in PostgreSQL
3. JWT tokens for mobile app authentication
4. Session cookies for web browser
5. 2FA (Two-Factor Auth) via SMS or authenticator app
6. OAuth for third-party apps ("Login with Instagram")
7. Rate limiting: 200 requests/hour per user
```

### Amazon E-commerce Authentication

```
1. Email + password with bcrypt hashing
2. MFA (Multi-Factor Auth) for sensitive operations
3. Session-based for web, JWT for mobile/APIs
4. Separate authentication for Seller Central
5. Federated identity for AWS services (IAM, Cognito)
6. Device fingerprinting for fraud detection
7. Step-up authentication for payments
```

sections.title: 9. Security Best Practices
sections.body:
### The Security Checklist ✅

```
Password Security:
  ✅ Hash with bcrypt (cost factor 12+)
  ✅ Enforce minimum password length (8+ chars)
  ✅ Check against breached password databases
  ❌ NEVER store plain text passwords
  ❌ NEVER use MD5 or SHA1 for passwords

Token Security:
  ✅ Short-lived access tokens (15-30 minutes)
  ✅ Long-lived refresh tokens (stored securely)
  ✅ HTTPS only (never send tokens over HTTP)
  ✅ Store tokens in HTTP-only cookies (not localStorage)
  ❌ NEVER put sensitive data in JWT payload
  ❌ NEVER use JWT without expiration

API Security:
  ✅ Rate limiting (prevent brute force)
  ✅ CORS configuration (prevent cross-site attacks)
  ✅ Input validation (prevent injection)
  ✅ SQL parameterized queries
  ✅ Request size limits
  ❌ NEVER expose stack traces in production
  ❌ NEVER trust client-side data
```

### Rate Limiting — Preventing Abuse

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, HTTPException
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
import redis

app = FastAPI()
redis_client = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379)

async def rate_limit(request: Request, max_requests: int = 100, window: int = 3600):
    """Limit to max_requests per window (seconds)"""
    client_ip = request.client.host
    key = f"rate_limit:{client_ip}"

    current = redis_client.get(key)
    if current and int(current) >= max_requests:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=429, detail="Too many requests")

    pipe = redis_client.pipeline()
    pipe.incr(key)
    pipe.expire(key, window)
    pipe.execute()
```

sections.title: 10. Implementation Patterns
sections.body:
### Pattern 1: The Complete Auth Middleware (FastAPI)

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, HTTPException
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
import time

app = FastAPI()

# CORS - Control which domains can access your API
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["https://yourfrontend.com"],  # Not "*" in production!
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)

# Auth middleware - runs on every request
@app.middleware("http")
async def auth_middleware(request: Request, call_next):
    # Skip auth for public endpoints
    public_paths = ["/login", "/register", "/health", "/docs"]
    if request.url.path in public_paths:
        return await call_next(request)

    # Check for token
    auth_header = request.headers.get("Authorization")
    if not auth_header or not auth_header.startswith("Bearer "):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Missing authentication")

    token = auth_header.split(" ")[1]
    try:
        user_data = verify_token(token)
        request.state.user = user_data
    except Exception:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Invalid token")

    response = await call_next(request)
    return response
```

### Pattern 2: Multi-Auth Support

```python
# Support both JWT and API Key authentication
from fastapi import Security, HTTPException
from fastapi.security import HTTPBearer, APIKeyHeader

bearer_scheme = HTTPBearer(auto_error=False)
api_key_header = APIKeyHeader(name="X-API-Key", auto_error=False)

async def get_current_user(
    bearer: Optional[str] = Security(bearer_scheme),
    api_key: Optional[str] = Security(api_key_header)
):
    # Try JWT first
    if bearer:
        return verify_jwt_token(bearer.credentials)

    # Then try API key
    if api_key:
        return verify_api_key(api_key)

    raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Not authenticated")
```

sections.title: Summary: Which Auth Method to Use?
sections.body:
```
Building a web app?
├── Traditional server-rendered → Session-based auth
└── Modern SPA (React/Vue) → JWT tokens

Building a mobile app?
└── JWT tokens (access + refresh)

Building an API for developers?
└── API keys + JWT for user context

Need "Login with Google"?
└── OAuth 2.0

Need different user permissions?
└── RBAC (Role-Based Access Control)

Building microservices?
└── JWT tokens (stateless, any service can verify)
```
